Data Types and Type Coercion
topics.content:
### How JavaScript Thinks About Data

JavaScript has 8 data types, divided into **primitives** (stored by value) and **objects** (stored by reference).

#### The 7 Primitive Types

```javascript
// 1. undefined — variable declared but not assigned
let x;
console.log(x);           // undefined
console.log(typeof x);    // 'undefined'

// 2. null — intentional absence of value
const user = null;        // "there's no user here"
console.log(typeof null); // 'object' — this is a historical bug in JS!

// 3. boolean
const isLoggedIn = true;
console.log(typeof isLoggedIn); // 'boolean'

// 4. number — ALL numbers are 64-bit floating point (IEEE 754)
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);  // 0.30000000000000004 (!)
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3); // false — floating point trap
console.log(Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON); // true — correct comparison

console.log(Infinity);    // Infinity (1/0)
console.log(NaN);         // NaN (Not a Number — e.g., 'abc' * 2)
console.log(NaN === NaN); // false (!!) — NaN is never equal to itself
console.log(Number.isNaN(NaN)); // true — use this instead of === NaN

// 5. string
const greeting = 'Hello';
const template = `Hello, ${greeting}!`;  // Template literals
console.log(typeof greeting);   // 'string'

// 6. symbol — unique, immutable identifier
const id1 = Symbol('id');
const id2 = Symbol('id');
console.log(id1 === id2); // false — every Symbol is unique
const key = Symbol('key');
const obj = { [key]: 'secret' };  // Symbol as object key

// 7. bigint — integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
const big = 9007199254740991n;  // Add n suffix
console.log(big + 1n);          // 9007199254740992n
// console.log(big + 1);        // TypeError: can't mix bigint and number
```

#### Objects (Stored by Reference)

```javascript
// Primitives: copy by value
let a = 5;
let b = a;  // b gets a copy of the value
b = 10;
console.log(a); // 5 — a is unchanged

// Objects: copy by reference
const obj1 = { count: 5 };
const obj2 = obj1;   // obj2 points to the SAME object
obj2.count = 10;
console.log(obj1.count); // 10 — obj1 was modified!

// To copy an object, use spread or Object.assign
const obj3 = { ...obj1 };  // shallow copy
obj3.count = 99;
console.log(obj1.count);   // still 10 — separate copy now
```

#### Type Coercion — JavaScript's Most Surprising Feature

JavaScript automatically converts types in certain operations. This is the source of most "JS is weird" examples.

```javascript
// == performs type coercion (almost always avoid this)
0 == false;        // true  — 0 coerced to false
'' == false;       // true  — '' coerced to false
'0' == false;      // true
null == undefined; // true  — special case
null == 0;         // false — null only equals undefined
[] == false;       // true  — [] → '' → 0 → false

// === performs NO coercion (always use this)
0 === false;       // false
'' === false;      // false

// The + operator: addition OR string concatenation
1 + 2;             // 3     — both numbers
'1' + 2;           // '12'  — number coerced to string
1 + '2';           // '12'
1 + 2 + '3';       // '33'  — 1+2=3, then 3+'3'='33'
'1' + 2 + 3;       // '123' — '1'+2='12', then '12'+3='123'

// Other operators coerce to numbers
'5' - 2;           // 3
'5' * '2';         // 10
true + 1;          // 2    — true coerced to 1
false + 1;         // 1    — false coerced to 0
null + 1;          // 1    — null coerced to 0
undefined + 1;     // NaN  — undefined coerced to NaN

// Falsy values — these all evaluate to false in boolean context
Boolean(false);     // false
Boolean(0);         // false
Boolean(-0);        // false
Boolean(0n);        // false — BigInt zero
Boolean('');        // false
Boolean(null);      // false
Boolean(undefined); // false
Boolean(NaN);       // false

// Everything else is truthy — including these surprises!
Boolean([]);       // true  — empty array!
Boolean({});       // true  — empty object!
Boolean('0');      // true  — non-empty string!
Boolean('false');  // true  — non-empty string!
```

**The rules to remember**: always use `===`. When checking if a value is "empty", be explicit: `value === null`, `value === undefined`, `value.length === 0`.
